passage: The nurse's room at the school in Lagos had a chart with little faces from smiling to crying. Ada sat on the bed holding her stomach. “Where does it hurt?” asked the nurse. Ada pointed to the left side. “What kind of pain?” “Like a twist.” “How strong? Point to a face.” Ada pointed to the middle face. Yosef, her cousin, said, “She said it was nothing at breakfast.” Ada looked at her shoes. “I didn't want a fuss.” The nurse nodded. “I'm glad you told me now. I'll call your aunt so a doctor can look if it keeps going.”

qa.q: Where did Ada point to when the nurse asked where it hurt?
qa.a: To the left side of her stomach.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt about the pain at breakfast, and how do you know?
qa.a: She was probably reluctant to worry anyone and a little embarrassed, since she looked at her shoes and said, "I didn't want a fuss."

qa.q: What did the nurse do that helped Ada describe the pain?
qa.a: The nurse asked for the place, the kind and how strong, using a chart of faces.

qa.q: How might Yosef have felt about telling the nurse what Ada said?
qa.a: Yosef probably felt worried about Ada and wanted her to get help. 🙂

grounding: A child describes pain by place, kind and level using a chart, and some children downplay pain to avoid fuss.

passage: In the clinic waiting room at the community centre, Francis waited with his mother while a volunteer, Ankita, handed out colouring sheets. When the nurse called his name, he winced as he stood. “Show me on the picture of a body where it hurts,” said the nurse. Francis coloured a spot on his ankle red. “Is it sharp or dull?” “Sharp, like a pinch.” “How big? Small, medium or big?” “Medium.” He had been limping for days and telling everyone he was fine. His mother said quietly, “You told me you were fine.” Francis stared at the floor. “I didn't want to miss football.”

qa.q: Where did Francis colour the spot on the body picture?
qa.a: On his ankle.

qa.q: Why did Francis tell everyone he was fine?
qa.a: He did not want to miss football, so he downplayed the pain.

qa.q: What could Francis's mother and the nurse do next?
qa.a: They could listen to how the ankle feels, and check with the doctor since he had been limping and the pain kept going.

qa.q: How might Ankita, the volunteer, see the scene?
qa.a: Ankita may see a boy who is hurting and worried, and can help by offering a calm, friendly space while he waits.

grounding: A child describes pain by place, kind and size, and downplays it to avoid missing football, so changed behaviour deserves attention.

passage: I'm Vikas, and my sister Disha had a tummy ache on Saturday. Mummy asked her where it hurt, and Disha just said, “Everywhere.” Then Mummy got a paper and drew a big circle for a tummy. “Point. And what kind: sharp like a pin, or squeezing, or burning?” Disha pointed low on the right side. “Sharp. Like a pin that stays.” “How bad, one to five?” Disha held up four fingers. I'd never seen her say four about anything; she once fell off her cycle and said two. Mummy's face went serious, and she took Disha to the clinic that afternoon. I don't know what the doctor said, but Mummy said Disha had explained it really well.

qa.q: Where did Disha point on the drawing?
qa.a: Disha pointed low on the right side.

qa.q: What was Disha likely feeling when she held up four fingers?
qa.a: Disha was likely in real pain and worried, since she usually plays pain down.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Disha describe the pain?
qa.a: She drew a tummy for pointing, offered words for the kind of pain and asked for a number, then acted the same afternoon.

qa.q: Why did Vikas notice the number four?
qa.a: Vikas knew Disha usually plays pain down, like saying two after falling off her cycle, so four seemed serious.

grounding: Shows a child describing pain by place, kind and level with a drawing and a scale, and an adult taking it seriously.

passage: Monday: Sarika rubbed her ear at breakfast. When her mother, Sharmila, asked, she said, “It's nothing,” and ran for the bus. The dance show was on Saturday, and she wasn't missing it. Wednesday: At practice she kept tilting her head, and at home she didn't want her favourite crunchy snack. Sharmila noticed. “Show me where it hurts, and how much, one to five.” Sarika pointed inside her left ear. “Three. It throbs when I chew.” “Three since Monday?” Sarika nodded, eyes down. “I didn't want a fuss.” Thursday: The doctor looked in her ear and gave her medicine. By Saturday, she danced.

qa.q: Which ear hurt?
qa.a: Her left ear hurt.

qa.q: Why did Sarika say “It's nothing” on Monday?
qa.a: Sarika was worried a fuss would make her miss the dance show on Saturday, so she hid the pain.

qa.q: What made Sharmila check more closely on Wednesday?
qa.a: She noticed Sarika's changed behaviour, tilting her head and refusing her favourite snack, and asked where and how much it hurt.

qa.q: What was the week like for Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila had to watch for clues because Sarika was hiding the pain, and she took her to the doctor once the signs were clear.

grounding: Shows a child downplaying pain to avoid a fuss, and changed behaviour leading an adult to ask about place and level.

passage: Pankaj, you've been rubbing your jaw all day and saying “it's fine”. Let your Hafsa Nani tell you what happened to me. When I was eleven, a back tooth started to ache. I didn't tell anyone; the dentist in our town had a drill that sounded like a tractor. I chewed on the other side. I said “fine” for three weeks. Then one night my cheek swelled up like a mango, and my father carried me to the dentist anyway. He said it was much worse than it would have been. After that, my mother made a rule: say where it hurts, what kind of hurt and how much, even if it's small. So, Pankaj. Where, what kind, how much?

qa.q: What did the dentist's drill sound like to young Hafsa?
qa.a: It sounded like a tractor.

qa.q: Why did young Hafsa keep saying “fine” for three weeks?
qa.a: Young Hafsa was scared of the dentist's loud drill, so she hid the toothache to avoid the fuss.

qa.q: What rule did Hafsa's mother make, and why is it useful?
qa.a: To say where it hurts, what kind of hurt and how much, even if it's small, so problems are noticed early.

qa.q: What was that night like for Hafsa's father?
qa.a: He was probably worried when her cheek swelled and carried her to the dentist straight away.

grounding: Shows a child downplaying pain to avoid the clinic, and learning to describe pain by place, kind and level.

passage:
Exams started on Monday, and the clinic was two bus rides away in town, a trip that meant Amma losing a day's wages. So when her tummy hurt on Thursday, Kalyani said nothing. On Friday she said, "It's nothing."

But Ira didi noticed she'd left her rice, and that she kept pressing her right side when she thought no one was looking. Didi sat down beside her. "Show me where. Is it sharp, or dull, or cramping? If five is the worst ever, how bad?"

Kalyani pointed low on her right side. "Sharp. Four. Since yesterday."

Didi's face went serious. "Thank you for telling me properly. That's not a keep-quiet pain. I'm getting Amma, and we're going to the clinic today."

qa.q: Where did Kalyani point to?
qa.a: Low on her right side.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani keep saying "It's nothing"?
qa.a: She was worried about causing a fuss: the clinic was far, Amma would lose a day's wages and exams were coming, so she played the pain down.

qa.q: How did Ira didi help Kalyani describe the pain?
qa.a: She asked where it was, what kind it was and how bad on a scale of five, so Kalyani could say, "Sharp. Four. Since yesterday."

qa.q: What made Ira didi notice something was wrong?
qa.a: The change in behaviour: Kalyani left her rice and kept pressing her side when she thought no one was looking.

grounding: It shows a child playing down pain to avoid fuss, and an older sister noticing changed behaviour, helping her describe place, kind and level, and acting that day.
